text: Lesson 25 covered how to form a good hypothesis. Forming it is only the first stage of a larger, repeating cycle real hunt teams run every time -- and skipping a stage, or treating this as something you run once, is the most common way a hunting program quietly stops producing anything useful.

Four stages: form a hypothesis, gather data, analyze, and document findings. Then, whether or not that hunt found anything, refine and repeat. This is the actual day-to-day shape of a hunting program, the same way the NIST lifecycle from Chapter 1 is the shape of incident response -- a structure you run every time, not a one-off exercise.

Take the rundll32.exe hypothesis from Lesson 25. Gather data means pulling every rundll32.exe launch across the environment, with full command-line arguments, over a defined window. Analyze means baselining what normal usage looks like here, then filtering for a DLL path pointing at Downloads or Temp instead of System32.

It's tempting to treat a hunt that finds nothing as wasted effort, but that's the wrong read. A documented hunt with a clean result still confirms that, as of now, that specific technique isn't present in the environment -- genuinely useful information for the SOC's risk picture, and very different from never having looked at all.

The refine-and-repeat stage is what makes this a loop instead of a checklist. A confirmed hit feeds directly into the next lesson: turning it into a permanent detection. A clean result still refines the program -- maybe the window was too short, maybe the baseline needs more data, maybe it's time for a new hypothesis.

Either way, the team goes back to stage one with a sharper or new hypothesis, which is exactly why threat hunting is described as an ongoing practice, not a task any SOC ever finishes. Next: using the MITRE ATT&CK framework you already know as a map for deciding what to hunt for next.
